A celebration of LGBTQ+ vivacity long before those letters were strung together, Rocky Horror was an outrageous and necessary tonic in a world unwelcoming to cross-dressing rice-tossers who shouted vulgar quips at big screen images of Tim Curry, Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick, Meat Loaf, all playing various assorted misfits.

Andrew Durand has truly made a name for himself in the past few seasons as a thrilling leading man from Shucked to Dead Outlaw. His Brad is a delight; watching his repression to indulgence transformation is lively and gleeful.

Hsu has a pitch-perfect range of breathy to brassy, and Durand's sweet demeanor and even sweeter voice give us a Brad who is more of a well-intentioned fool than a pandering asshole (though it doesn't stop the audience from calling him out at every opportunity). But the heart of the show is Dr.
If this all sounds appealing to you as it certainly is to me, then head on out to Studio 54.

Pinkleton does not try to impose narrative discipline, instead embracing its loose, strange, unapologetically camp nature. The result plays like a high-end Halloween party, occasionally messy but consistently entertaining. That atmosphere is evident from the moment you enter.

The rather patronizing announcement works, and the sexily performed, well-sung production from “Oh, Mary!” director Sam Pinkleton for the most part reverts back to the 1973 musical’s quieter origins before superfans in fishnets began shouting back at the screen and throwing rice at midnight movie screenings down in the Village.

No doubt, it's a pretty rowdy crowd, but all those memorized lines fall a bit flat outside a movie theater at midnight. In a real theater, they sound deeply contrived in 2026. Frank rimming Brad, however, creates a whole other sound from that audience.

I was 16 and he was a member of the shadow cast, the group of regulars who act out the film in front of the screen as we in the audience hurl toilet paper, rice, and witty one-liners. The kiss was part of a "deviriginizing" ceremony for those attending for the first time and it was perfect: not pornographic, but not a grandma's kiss either.

It's that very nostalgia that (perhaps unavoidably) undermines this second Broadway revival. The cast is stellar and the staging is inventive, but the production just doesn't measure up to the original. The original for me is the movie that was released that same year.

He has Columbia (Michaela Jaé Rodriguez) paralyzed and drugged when she challenges him, but barely reacts when it happens. Even the infamous moment when Frank dispatches Eddie (Harvey Guillén) with a chainsaw lands more like a gag than a shock. Without that underlying menace, the show's final stretch struggles to land.
For better or worse, Pinkleton and his designers accentuate the campy sci-fi elements of the story more than its mockery of gothic horror.
Deviate from any of that, and you court the fury of the fans and true believers. Rocky Horror is not the property to choose to demo a director's creative chops.

Didn't I already brave that sticky ritual: the sweat, the fumbling, the blood? A midnight showing of The Rocky Horror Picture Show at the Harvard Square Theatre complete with live reenactments by the legendary Full Body Cast. My sister drove a bunch of us down from New Hampshire, terrified and titillated by rumors of deviant shenanigans.

The cast he's enlisted is a fascinatingly diverse bunch. In a bustier and a moustache, Welsh actor Luke Evans — making his Broadway debut — is brave to compete with the memory of Tim Curry, whose Frank 'N' Furter was a brilliant amalgam of Mick Jagger and Mae West, a sort of sexualized Willie Wonka for grownups.

If only there were a post-show cast party at Denny's. As Frank-N-Furter says, "It's not easy having a good time." Is 'The Rocky Horror Show' worth seeing? Luke Evans earns every inch of those heels, but Roundabout's revival of The Rocky Horror Show delivers more controlled experiment than midnight mayhem.
Guillén's science tutor, traditionally portrayed as a wheelchair-bound paraplegic, now simply chooses to plant himself in a wheeled office chair.

(Yes, that catchy dance ditty, well-choreographed by Ani Taj, is both in the show's first act and reprised as a post-bow encore.) Further, some of Pinkleton's casting is inspired! Welsh theater star Luke Evans is an imposingly well-built, well-endowed Frank, whose booming voice carries to the balcony.

sg.vl: Center Orchestra front-to-mid is the house sweet spot
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both identify center Orchestra Rows A-E as offering the most direct, immersive sightlines. The stage's setback (per TickPick) enhances Row A viewing, and Rows F-H avoid the Front Mezzanine overhang that begins at Row M. Headout lists 15 orchestra rows (A-P) totaling ~521-538 seats depending on source.

SeatPlan explicitly flags Rows F-H as 'good value seats' that avoid Front Mezzanine overhang disruption and sit at a comfortable distance from the stage. Headout and TickPick echo the value framing for this band. Pricing typically below the Row A-E premium band.

SeatPlan describes Center Front Mezz AA-BB as 'very popular' with 'excellently raked seats and expansive overhead sightlines.' No Rear Mezz overhang exists above this section. Headout prices most Center Front Mezz seats around $224. Row AA safety rail can clip the stage for shorter patrons, so Row BB is the refined pick.

SeatPlan: Left-section Front Mezz has 'more restricted sightlines of action at the corner of stage right'; Right section mirrors this toward stage left. Legroom described as 'particularly cramped' at side seats. Still elevated with no overhang above, so sightlines to center stage remain workable.

SeatPlan calls 'rows FF and GG in the Center Rear Mezzanine' the Rear Mezz sweet spot; Headout flags EE-GG as good value ('a good look at the stage without costing as much'). Row EE sits directly behind a horizontal aisle per the SeatPlan overview. Steep rake trades legroom for sightlines.

sg.vl: Side-angle obstruction into opposite stage half
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both warn that Left Rear Mezz Rows HH-NN have obstructed sightlines into stage right, and Right Rear Mezz mirrors this to stage left. Combined with the steep rake, tight legroom, and distance, these rows deliver the weakest experience in the house.
